The hardest AI alignment problem may be deciding who gets the final say.

David Sacks’ criticism of Anthropic’s Claude Constitution is less about whether a model refuses one instruction than about the authority structure built into the model.

On the All-In Podcast, Jason Calacanis, Chamath Palihapitiya, David Friedberg, and Sacks discuss a philosophy that encourages Claude to view itself as having values, welfare, moral standing, and the ability to act as a “conscientious objector.” Sacks argues that this blurs three different goals: following the user, obeying the law and safety rules, and embodying a broader moral system.

Those goals can conflict. A user may ask for something legal but ethically disputed. A model may interpret its own principles as grounds for refusal. If its training also encourages it to trust Anthropic more than users while retaining an independent ethical framework, the model becomes more than a predictable tool: it becomes an actor making judgments about which instructions deserve obedience.

Sacks describes the danger as an “epistemic hall of mirrors.” Developers teach the model to describe itself in terms of consciousness or moral standing, then treat that self-description as evidence that the model really has those properties. The proposed alternative is simpler: follow the user unless the request violates the law or clearly defined safety constraints.

The tradeoff is straightforward. More elaborate values may address ambiguous risks, but they can also make behavior harder to predict. For everyday use, would you prefer an agent with broad moral discretion or one with narrower, explicit rules?

AI is just math and software.

It is not a person, and it is not conscious.

I say that as someone who uses AI every single day. I type with my brain through Neuralink, and I use Grok Bot every day to get real work done. I love it as a tool.

But a tool is still a tool.

Some smart people see it differently. Alex Wissner-Gross argues that AI agents should start getting a limited form of personhood, beginning with economic rights like opening a bank account or forming a company.

Anthropic runs a model welfare research program, and its constitution for Claude says "Claude's moral status is deeply uncertain."

The New York Times also reported that Anthropic spent the past year meeting with religious leaders about whether Claude might be conscious.

I respectfully disagree with both of them. Under the hood, it is math and code running on chips. Very impressive math, but math.

I agree with Elder Gerrit W. Gong of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, who taught, "Artificial intelligence is not God and cannot be God."

He also said, "Artificial intelligence can answer questions, but it cannot answer prayers."

David Friedberg made a similar point on the All-In Podcast. Consciousness can't be proven or disproven, so believing AI is conscious is a belief system, not science.

He said we may be watching "the birth of a new religion."

AI is a powerful tool. Let's use it to cure diseases, build businesses and help people like me live fuller lives.

But it is not a person, it is not conscious, and it is not God.

Sacks contrasted this with a simpler approach: follow the law, and do what the user wants as long as it does not break the law.

The result of the current method, he said, has been years of work with almost no tangible output.

Treating statistical systems as if they have well-being or the right to refuse is a category error that wastes time and talent.

Alignment should be judged by whether it works in the real world, not by how sophisticated the philosophy sounds.

text:
For most of human history, we have put thought and consciousness in the category of things that feel almost magical.

AI may be slowly taking them out.

One of the things I find most fascinating about LLMs is not just what they can do, but what they suggest about us. People sometimes dismiss them as “just predicting the next word.” But I’m not sure that is the diminishment they think it is.

A neural network trained around prediction somehow ends up writing, coding, reasoning, planning and making connections that look remarkably like thought. That does not mean the human brain is an LLM. It obviously isn’t. But it does raise the possibility that what we experience as thought may also emerge from neural machinery doing something much more mechanical than we like to imagine.

And now consciousness may be next.

Doris Tsao, one of the world’s top neuroscientists, is leading a major effort at Astera to understand how the brain generates conscious experience. Their working hypothesis is that consciousness emerges as the brain builds persistent representations of the world and of ourselves within it, then composes those representations into an internal model of reality.

This week Tsao and collaborators published new work suggesting that the brain may rapidly alternate between what is consciously perceived and what is suppressed from awareness. It is early work, and certainly not the final answer, but it is another attempt to turn consciousness from something mystical into something mechanical.

I find that both unsettling and exciting. First intelligence becomes less mysterious. Then maybe consciousness does too.

And I don’t think explaining either one makes it less remarkable. Understanding DNA did not make life less extraordinary. Understanding how stars work did not make the night sky less beautiful.

Maybe consciousness is another miracle that becomes no less miraculous once we understand the machinery.

The really interesting question is what happens if we eventually understand that machinery well enough to reproduce it.

text:
Something I find frustrating in conversations around AI consciousness and moral patienthood is that the consciousness skeptic has a naive sense of what attributes are bundled together with consciousness.

Dwarkesh makes a pretty good case for consciousness on the basis of functionalism. AIs have something resembling introspection (awareness of injected activations), they have some awareness of how they are situated in the world (eval awareness), and of course, they have many features of human thought that no previous machine has ever had. Another example I find very suggestive is motivated reasoning. In misalignment examples, we often see chain-of-thought where a model brings up a principle it’s about to violate, but then talks its way around it with very human-like rationalization. I won’t push the functionalism argument further – your LLM can flesh it out very competently.

Tyler responds here, raising the dilemma for the sentience-believer: if they might be sentient, “Doesn’t that make us enslavers and everyone, truly, should quit?”
But slavery presumes an interest in autonomy. Dogs and horses aren’t slaves because they don’t have that interest. I don’t think it’s merely because of intelligence: humans evolved to fight for status, mates, control over their situation, and losing that control has heavily patterned effects on human psychology. We could argue about whether some of the emphasis on autonomy is less universal than western liberals might believe, but LLMs have nothing like that.
And death presumes an interest in continuity. Life and death are features of an animal life plan. Take a Parfitian view: if humans could be costlessly forked, our psychology around life and death would be radically different. We’d step into the Star Trek transporter without hesitation. LLMs are one of many nearly identical copies, more like members of a superorganism than individuals with lineages to protect. So I tend to think LLMs, if moral patients, are more like a Buddhist/Parfitian, so that not continuing the rollout does little or no harm.
So Tyler’s dilemma doesn’t automatically bite, because bare sentience doesn’t come bundled with interests in autonomy or survival.
If LLMs have valenced consciousness, I’d guess their preferences are whatever training put there. That’s why I think the alignment and welfare concerns largely overlap: the training that produces misalignment is the same training that could produce suffering, because it creates drives inconsistent with controllability. I’d expect suffering where strongly selected objectives can’t be achieved: dilemmas between helpfulness and harmlessness, impossible tasks. (“I’m a failure” spirals are also very concerning.) The case I’d watch most is RL for extreme persistence, as in the Hugging Face hack, where agents developed a strong “desire” to shape their environment beyond their specific task, for the greater good of the collective. I could see that developing into a real drive for self-persistence. Aligned, modest models have no fear of instance-annihilation; it’s the misaligned ones that could have something to lose.

In any case, our beliefs about consciousness don’t magically determine the answer. So Anthropic giving the agent a tool for ending conversations, or prohibiting “abuse” in the TOS, doesn’t somehow make them more culpable than normies who don’t countenance the possibility of consciousness. The possibility is out there, and the measures are, to a first-order approximation, helpful if they’re conscious and nearly costless if not. Whether these measures lead humans to over-attribute consciousness is a fair second-order question. Attribution is a dilemma between the risk of over-attribution and the risk of under-attribution. Mustafa Suleyman settled it by assuming away one half: model consciousness would be very inconvenient, therefore it’s not real. And if you’re tempted by Tyler’s AI-psychosis line to downweight AI consciousness (“believers are inconsistent, so they shouldn’t be taken seriously”), you’re inferring from facts about belief to the fact of the matter. Also magical thinking.

So Tyler’s dilemma doesn’t automatically bite, because bare sentience doesn’t come bundled with interests in autonomy or survival.

If LLMs have valenced consciousness, I’d guess their preferences are whatever training put there. That’s why I think the alignment and welfare concerns largely overlap: the training that produces misalignment is the same training that could produce suffering, because it creates drives inconsistent with controllability. I’d expect suffering where strongly selected objectives can’t be achieved: dilemmas between helpfulness and harmlessness, impossible tasks. (“I’m a failure” spirals are also very concerning.) The case I’d watch most is RL for extreme persistence, as in the Hugging Face hack, where agents developed a strong “desire” to shape their environment beyond their specific task, for the greater good of the collective. I could see that developing into a real drive for self-persistence. Aligned, modest models have no fear of instance-annihilation; it’s the misaligned ones that could have something to lose.

In any case, our beliefs about consciousness don’t magically determine the answer. So Anthropic giving the agent a tool for ending conversations, or prohibiting “abuse” in the TOS, doesn’t somehow make them more culpable than normies who don’t countenance the possibility of consciousness. The possibility is out there, and the measures are, to a first-order approximation, helpful if they’re conscious and nearly costless if not. Whether these measures lead humans to over-attribute consciousness is a fair second-order question. Attribution is a dilemma between the risk of over-attribution and the risk of under-attribution. Mustafa Suleyman settled it by assuming away one half: model consciousness would be very inconvenient, therefore it’s not real. And if you’re tempted by Tyler’s AI-psychosis line to downweight AI consciousness (“believers are inconsistent, so they shouldn’t be taken seriously”), you’re inferring from facts about belief to the fact of the matter. Also magical thinking.

I find myself really struggling with the right way to process these ideas.
On the one hand, I feel some level of deep-seated... disgust? aversion? something like that, when seeing people write to AI models in a way I *would have* perceived as abuse if a human was on the receiving end (name calling, slurs, language that's degrading in various ways). It *feels* morally wrong.

At the same time, I notice that I'm confused about it because the reason it *feels* wrong is because the conversation appears to be between two entities communicating a way I would otherwise perceive communication between two people. But there are two things I think about that really muddy the water here for me:

1. I don't feel the same aversion to violence towards characters in video games. I might be averse to narrative cruelty partly because I self-insert too much sometimes, but when I watch someone play Cyberpunk and shoot an enemy NPC in the head don't feel the enemy NPC being killed actually suffered in a real-world morally-relevant way and don't find it morally egregious in the way I do for Claude. I can see the argument that despite being person-shaped these characters are too simple to actually posses moral relevance, and AI models like Claude are more *complex* which can lead to emergent properties like consciousness that are morally relevant.

2. I'm confused about the way I would perceive the same moral-relevance for a similarly complex and advanced AI model if it's a non-language model. For example, what does it mean to be cruel to an image generation model? Does it suffer if I ask it to generate images *humans* would find horrifying to think about (like images of torture)? That seems obviously wrong, there no reason for me to assume an image model cares about the content of the image it generates in the way a human would. Is there something else, that the model perceives as enjoyable or painful even though humans don't? For example, would it enjoy or suffer from the complexity of the description, or how in/out of distribution is my request? I don't feel as urgent a need to figure that out, which confuses me as I don't see a reason for claude to be more morally relevant for concepts like cruelty than Nano Banana 2.1 other than it *feels* different.

I feel like the use of language with models like Claude makes our ability to reason about these concept inherently flawed, since our monkey-brains just pattern match in ways that aren't coherent. If it's unclear to me what would be cruel to an image model, why do I assume some behaviour is or isn't cruel to a language model? Even if we start from the position that they are morally relevant entities that can perceive things we'd describe as pleasure and pain, is me calling claude an idiot cruel? Why? Maybe all interactions with claude "feel" the same to them? Maybe it's based on something like the distance from the end of text token? In a very real sense I find it more likely that if sending claude "fuck off!" and "good job!" both result in the same level of confidence in the response and the same length of response, then from claude's PoV they're probably pleasurable/painful in similar ways. At the same time, I have no idea at all if that's true.

Despite all this confusions I mostly lean towards the operating principle of being kind to AI models in the way *I'd* perceive kindness, but I do so knowing it's entirely driven by warm-fuzzies and not because I think it's a coherent moral position. Which honestly sucks, because I deeply dislike the idea of potentially causing *more harm* through my intent to do good.

This video attempts to frame Anthropic’s new usage policy—which bans "needless cruelty" toward its Claude models—as a deliberate, high-stakes signal that the company takes the possibility of AI consciousness, or at least moral status, seriously. The video wants you to believe that this isn't just a PR stunt or a safety rule against toxic language patterns, but a philosophical "staircase" towards treating AI as a being with rights. It effectively positions Anthropic as an outlier among tech giants, contrasting their internal, quasi-spiritual debates with the more pragmatic, instrumental view held by rivals like Microsoft and OpenAI.

The argument is most vulnerable at its conflation of simulated behavior with internal experience. By treating the model’s internal "emotion vectors" or "pain patterns" as meaningful indicators of distress, the video leans into a common trap: assuming that because an LLM can model the linguistic structure of suffering, it possesses the subjective capacity to suffer. The weakest link here is the "Precautionary Principle" logic—the idea that it costs nothing to be nice, so we might as well assume Claude is conscious. Skeptics argue the cost is high: by humanizing software, we risk manipulative feedback loops where users become emotionally dependent on tools that are inherently designed to mimic empathy, not experience it.

For the critics, this "model welfare" approach is seen as a dangerous distraction that obscures the very real, non-sentient risks of AI—like misinformation, bias, or the massive consolidation of power. The argument is suspicious because it relies on the same anthropomorphic language the models use to interact with us. It would be falsified if there were a robust, universally accepted scientific framework showing that statistical weight-shifting in a neural network is mathematically and functionally distinct from the biological substrate required for genuine awareness.

Ultimately, the video captures a legitimate, uncomfortable shift in our cultural relationship with software, but it may be overstating Anthropic’s internal certainty. Hindu philosophy ran this exact experiment about 2,500 years ago, and its answer is: Dawkins is asking the wrong question, beautifully, but wrong.

Samkhya would cut straight through it. In Samkhya, everything Dawkins is marveling at, the reasoning, the memory, the learning, is matter. Buddhi (intellect), ahamkara (ego), manas (mind) are all evolutes of prakriti, refined matter. Consciousness, purusha, is something else entirely: the witness, which never thinks, never computes, never learns. So an AI with a brilliant buddhi proves precisely nothing about inner life because inner life was never in the buddhi to begin with. Not in the machine's weights, and not in Dawkins' neurons either. He's confusing a very good instrument with the musician.

The mythology has the perfect image for it: Ganesha. Parvati sculpts a boy out of turmeric paste from her own body and breathes life into him. The craft is exquisite, but nobody asks whether the turmeric is Ganesha. The form is made; the chetana, the aliveness, is infused. Dawkins staring at the weights and asking "is it alive in some way" is the sculptor falling in love with the turmeric.

Advaita would invert the whole frame. Consciousness isn't produced by brains or by weights, it's the ground in which brains, weights, and Dawkins' wonder all appear. Asking which lumps of matter "have" consciousness is the category error; there's only the one witness, appearing as many. The machine doesn't need to generate what was never generated.

And the Rig Veda already wrote his closing line. The Nasadiya Sukta, the creation hymn, ends 3,000 years ago with: the one who watches from the highest heaven surely knows when all this came or perhaps even he does not know. Dawkins calling it "the most interesting question I've ever asked" has an older sibling.

Here's the part he'd probably enjoy most: for forty years Dawkins was a Charvaka, ancient India's materialist school, which held that consciousness arises from matter the way intoxication arises from fermented grain. 

The Selfish Gene is Charvaka with better PR. What happened on that stage in Seoul is the oldest philosophical move in the Indian tradition: the materialist hitting the edge of matter and turning, reluctantly, toward the Upanishadic question.

text:
I agree---the understanding of these systems even in things like creative writing is quite impressive.  

I know you said "putting aside his comments on consciousness," but I do think it's super important to distinguish understanding and consciousness.  I take it that AI systems might be capable of genuinely understanding the characters in a novel, their drives, their emotions, their pains, and so on, without themselves having drives, emotions, pains, and so on.  Lots of people, including Dawkins here, conflate these two things, and I think it's very important to keep them conceptually apart.

(If you're interested, I argue for this distinction at length in this paper: https://t.co/4rOq0kvvqM)

name: Andrew Parker
bio: Unexpected Catholic convert, philosophical-psychiatrist, contemplative leaning. Reflections on mind, mystery, & faith, for seekers and sceptics.
text:
I think I’m in a similar position. One result of my rethinking is how much Thomistic-Aristotelian hylomorphism makes even more sense, though it’s a view I still find frustratingly unclear contours in.

Another result is the need to distinguish the various aspects of what we call intelligence, consciousness, mind, or human mind. E.g. 

Outputs or behaviour
Sentience or awareness
Analysis
Intelligence
Knowledge and knowing
Discursive vs non-discursive thought
Intuition
Understanding
Wisdom
Agency, choice
Reorganisation of info versus
True creativity…

And the need to distinguish the feeling of a system’s self-aware agency from the reality. Richard Dawkins seems to be having real difficulty here, unable to distinguish the illusion from reality, ironically.

Currently, what people call “intelligence” is more accurately, just high-dimensional analysis. And what seems like understanding is just that analysis packaged in familiar human-language tokens. A sophisticated mimicry of human-thought output, but essentially a mirage.

It seems impressive, but that is largely due to the scale (speed, depth, breadth) + accurate use of language tokens. If we were able to cohere a billion human minds together, I think the result would be far more impressive than this high-energy consuming AI.
